blocks.prompt: Pip Wakes the Garden
blocks.text: Every morning, a small fairy named Pip woke up inside a bluebell flower. Pip had wings as thin as glass. When the sun came up, the wings caught the light and turned pink and gold. Pip helped the garden wake up too. She tapped each closed flower so it would open. She woke the sleepy bees. In old stories, people left a little bowl of milk out at night to thank the fairies for their help. Pip liked those nights best of all.

blocks.prompt: The Rings in the Grass
blocks.text: Have you ever seen a circle of mushrooms in the grass? For hundreds of years, people had no idea what made them, so they made up a story. They said fairies had danced there all night in a ring, round and round, until the morning. When the fairies left, the ring of mushrooms was all that stayed behind. People called these circles fairy rings, and some were afraid to step inside one. We know the real answer now. A fairy ring is made by a fungus that grows under the ground. The fungus spreads out in a slow circle, feeding on the soil as it goes. Each year the circle grows a little wider. When the weather is damp, mushrooms pop up along the edge of the circle. Some fairy rings are tiny. Others are so old and so wide that they are bigger than a house. The dancing fairies were never real, but the rings are, and they are strange enough on their own.

blocks.prompt: The Little People of Many Lands
blocks.text: Almost every country in the world has stories about tiny magical people, and almost every country gives them a different name. In Ireland they were the good folk. In England small house fairies were called brownies, said to clean a home in secret while the family slept. In Scandinavia there were the huldufolk, the hidden people. The names change from place to place, but the idea repeats again and again: a small, secret people living just out of sight, in the woods, under hills, or beneath the floorboards. The old stories came with rules. People believed fairies could be helpful or dangerous, so they tried to stay on the good side of them. One common rule was about iron. Many stories said fairies hated iron and would not come near it, so a farmer might hang an iron horseshoe over a door to keep them out. Another rule was to be polite and never call them by their real name, which is why people used kind nicknames like the good folk. Some families left out a bowl of milk or a crust of bread at night as a small thank you. Why did so many faraway places invent such similar stories? No one is certain. Long ago, the world was dark at night and full of sounds no one could explain. A story about hidden people was one way to make sense of a noise in the woods, a missing tool, or a ring of mushrooms in the grass.

5.title: The Fairy in the Bluebell
5.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The Cottingley fairy photos were taken in 1917
The photographers were two young cousins in England

In the 1980s the cousins admitted the fairies were paper cutouts

blocks.prompt: The Photographs That Fooled the World
blocks.text: In the summer of 1917, in a village in England called Cottingley, two cousins borrowed a camera. Elsie Wright was sixteen. Frances Griffiths was nine. They walked down to the stream behind the house, and a little while later they came back with something astonishing: a photograph of Frances with four small winged fairies dancing in front of her. Over the next three years the girls produced five fairy photographs in all. The pictures might have stayed a family curiosity, but they reached the wrong, or perhaps the perfect, person. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, the famous author who invented the sharp-eyed detective Sherlock Holmes, saw the photographs and believed them completely. In 1920 he published them in a popular magazine along with an article arguing that fairies were real. If the man who created the world's most logical detective said so, many readers thought, then surely it must be true. For more than sixty years the Cottingley fairies were argued over. Then, in the early 1980s, the two women, now elderly, finally told the truth. The fairies were paper cutouts. Elsie had drawn them, copied in part from a children's book, and the cousins had held them up with hatpins stuck into the ground. They had never expected the joke to travel so far, and once a famous man had staked his name on it, they felt too embarrassed to confess. Even at the end, though, Frances insisted that one of the five photographs was genuine, and that they truly had seen fairies by the stream. That small claim keeps a door open, which may be exactly why the story refuses to die. A hoax that outlived the joke, and nearly outlived the jokers, has a strange magic all its own.

6.title: The Fairy in the Bluebell
6.subtitle: A reading and analysis sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Fairy belief appears across cultures for over a thousand years
In Iceland, road crews have rerouted work around huldufolk rocks
The changeling story once explained sudden childhood illness
Fairy rings are caused by a fungus, not by dancing
The Cottingley photographs were faked with paper and hatpins

blocks.prompt: Why We Keep Believing in Fairies
blocks.text: No one has ever caught a fairy, and yet fairies have never quite gone away. For at least a thousand years, across cultures that never met, people have told stories about a small, hidden race living alongside us, just beyond the edge of the firelight. The Irish called them the good folk. In Iceland they were the huldufolk, the hidden people, and belief in them was strong enough that road crews have, in living memory, rerouted construction to avoid disturbing rocks said to be their homes. The costumes change and the names change, but the character stays the same: something small, secret, and easily offended, sharing our world without quite belonging to it. Where did such a specific idea come from, in so many places at once? Part of the answer is that the old world was genuinely hard to explain. Milk soured overnight. Tools vanished and reappeared. A healthy child could sicken without warning, and grieving parents sometimes told themselves the fairies had swapped their baby for a changeling, a fairy child left in its place. It was a cruel comfort, but it was a comfort: a story that turned random misfortune into something with a cause and, sometimes, a cure. Even the strange rings of mushrooms that appear in fields had an explanation ready made. People said fairies had danced there in a circle through the night. The real cause, a fungus spreading outward underground and pushing up mushrooms at its edge, would not be understood for centuries. Until then, the dancing fairies were as good an answer as any. Belief also survived because it was useful, and because it was guarded by rules. Fairies were said to hate iron, so a horseshoe over the door became a small shield against bad luck. They were not to be named directly, so people called them the good folk to stay on their good side. A bowl of milk left out at night was cheap insurance. These customs asked little and promised protection, and habits like that are passed down long after anyone remembers exactly why. And then there is the simplest reason of all: we want to believe. The story of the Cottingley fairies proves how much. In 1917 two English cousins photographed themselves with paper fairies held up on hatpins, a childish prank. Yet Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, the brilliant man who invented Sherlock Holmes, championed the photographs as real, and thousands of readers agreed with him. The pictures were obvious fakes, and it did not matter. People believed because the world is a little more wonderful with fairies in it than without them. That wish is the true magic in every fairy story, and it is the one part no scientist has ever explained away.
